messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 39
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Construction Worker
  trauma_type: Witnessed other trauma
  pcl5: 73

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Suppress Anger: never allow myself to feel or express anger, Gambling: I gamble to distract myself or feel excitement, Dissociate Deliberately: deliberately try to leave my body or blank out
  Memory: Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images., Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Taste Vividness: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns
  Negative Appraisals: Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me, Inadequacy: I am inadequate

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

David is a 39-year-old construction worker who, until eight months ago, considered his life stable and predictable. The event that changed everything happened on a Tuesday, a day that started with the familiar scent of diesel and wet concrete. He was sharing a coffee with his colleague and friend, Marco, during a morning break, the two of them laughing about a football game from the weekend. The coffee was cheap and slightly burnt, a taste so routine it was comforting. When the break ended, Marco headed back up the scaffolding on the third story. David remained on the ground, coiling a power cord, when he heard a sharp crack, like a rifle shot, followed by a scream that was cut short. He looked up just in time to see Marco’s body silhouetted against the sky for a fraction of a second before he fell. The memory does not play like a film for David; it is a series of stark, silent photographs. The image of the fall. The image of the twisted scaffolding cable. The image of the aftermath on the ground.

In the weeks that followed, the sensory details of that moment began to intrude on his present. At the work site, the smell of dust would suddenly be replaced by a coppery, metallic scent he recognized as blood, and he would have to turn away, fighting nausea. The most persistent echo was the taste of that morning’s coffee. Now, whenever a memory fragment breaks through, he can taste the acrid, burnt grounds in the back of his throat, a flavour that arrives unbidden and can ruin any meal. He has come to believe that the world he once understood—one governed by safety regulations, predictability, and fairness—was a complete illusion. Now, he is certain that catastrophe is random and inevitable, and he is fundamentally powerless to prevent it. This feeling of helplessness is tied to a profound sense of personal failure; he watched his friend fall and did nothing. He knows logically there was nothing he could have done, but the feeling of inadequacy is absolute, a cold weight in his chest that tells him he failed in the most essential way a man can.

His life has been systematically reconfigured to manage these experiences. At work, when an image flashes or the phantom smell rises, he has learned to deliberately "check out." He will fix his gaze on a distant point, a rivet on a steel beam or a crack in the pavement, and force his mind to go blank, effectively leaving his body until the wave passes. His foreman has warned him twice about being "unresponsive" around heavy machinery. At home, in the evenings, a different kind of struggle unfolds. A deep, simmering rage sits within him—at the company, at the faulty cable, at the sheer bad luck of it all—but he is terrified of it. He has a firm conviction that if he were to ever express his anger, it would erupt uncontrollably and destroy what little he has left. So, he swallows it, maintaining a quiet, almost unnaturally calm demeanor that his wife, before she left him three months ago, called "living with a ghost."

The silence in his now-empty apartment became unbearable. To escape it, David started driving to a nearby casino after his shifts. The loud, vibrant, demanding environment was a perfect anesthetic. The focus required for poker or blackjack was the only thing that could reliably crowd out the intrusive images and the taste of burnt coffee. It offered a feeling of excitement and control that was entirely absent from the rest of his existence. What began as a distraction has become a compulsion, and the financial strain is mounting. David sought therapy after receiving a final written warning at his job and a desperate call from his ex-wife about his rapidly accumulating debts. He feels he is losing his grip on everything and came to his first session not with hope, but with a quiet desperation, stating that he doesn't know if he can be fixed but needs to find a way to "make the pictures stop."
